title: How to respond to a bad Airbnb review (with templates)
summary: How to respond to a bad Airbnb review: a four-part structure, copyable templates by complaint, what never to write, and when to dispute instead.
body_markdown:
[All posts](https://prohost.ai/blog)


**A bad review has two readers. One is the guest who wrote it, and that stay is over. The other is every future guest deciding whether to book you, and that one you can still reach. A public response is the only part of the review you control, and it sits under the guest's words for as long as the review does. Most hosts never write one. Here is how to write a response that the next guest trusts, with templates for the complaints that show up most often in 1, 2 and 3-star reviews.**


## Key takeaways


- **The response is for the next guest, not the last one.** Write it for someone comparing your listing with two others, not to win the argument.
- **Most bad reviews go unanswered.** On listings connected to ProhostAI, 11.8% of guest reviews got a public host response, about 1 in 8, and bad reviews get a response about as often as good ones.
- **Use four parts:** thank them, name the specific issue, say what you changed, and invite the next guest. Keep it under 100 words.
- **Value and accuracy are where bad reviews score lowest.** On 1 to 3-star reviews, value averaged 2.54 out of 5 and accuracy 2.98, below cleanliness (3.00) and well below check-in (3.68).
- **Get it right before you submit.** Airbnb[posts your response right away](https://www.airbnb.com/help/article/32) , so draft it, sleep on it, then post it.
- **If the review breaks Airbnb's policy, dispute it instead.**

## Where we're coming from


I spent 6 years at Airbnb as a staff data scientist on the hosting team, and today we host in Hawaii, the Smokies and Joshua Tree, with a[4.99 rating across thousands of guest stays](https://prohost.ai/about) . We've had the bad review too. ProhostAI has analyzed more than 180,000 guest reviews for the hosts on it, and the numbers below come from those reviews.


The pattern is consistent: hosts answer the ones that cost them bookings about as often as the warm 5-star reviews. A 5-star review doesn't need you. A 2-star review does.


*How we measured: response rate from 147,423 guest reviews published in the last 12 months; sub-scores from 6,134 guest reviews rated 1 to 3 stars on 3,449 listings over the same period. Internal workspaces excluded (read-only aggregate of ProhostAI data, November 2026).*


## Who the response is really for


The guest who left the review has already gone home. They will rarely read your reply, and if they do, it won't change their mind. The person who reads it is a stranger planning a trip, scrolling your reviews at 10 p.m., trying to decide if your place is safe to book.


That reader wants to know three things: is this a pattern or a one-off, did the host take it seriously, and would it happen to me. A calm, specific reply that names a fix answers all three. Correcting the guest's tone, explaining your week or quoting the house rules at length answers none of them.


## The four-part structure


1. **Thank them, briefly.** One short sentence. Not three lines of gratitude.
2. **Name the specific issue.** Use their words if you can. "You're right that the second bedroom was warmer than it should have been."
3. **Say what you changed.** This is the most important line. A fix is a fact the next guest can rely on: "We've added a portable AC unit to that room." If nothing needed changing, give the context instead, in one line.
4. **Invite the next guest.** Close with something the reader can use: "If you're planning a summer stay, the main bedroom has its own split system."


Keep it under 100 words. Use the guest's first name once at most, and never their last name.


## Response templates by complaint


The lowest average sub-scores on bad reviews tell you which complaints you'll answer most often: value, accuracy, cleanliness, communication and check-in. (Location averaged 3.66; you can't move the house, so the accuracy template covers it: make the listing say what the location is.) Here's a template for each, plus two situations that need their own approach.


### Value ("not worth the price")


Value averaged 2.54 on 1 to 3-star reviews, the lowest of any sub-score. It's about the price compared with what the guest expected.


> Thank you for staying with us, \[guest first name\]. We hear you on value. A \[number\]-night stay over \[holiday or event\] is priced at the top of our range, and the \[specific thing they mentioned\] should have matched that. We've \[specific change: replaced the sofa bed mattress / added a second coffee maker / updated the photos to show the room sizes\]. Guests looking for the best rate will find it \[midweek / outside the event dates\].


Don't defend the price with market comparisons. Tell the reader what's better now and when it's cheaper.


### Accuracy ("not as described")


Accuracy averaged 2.98. This is the complaint you can fix fastest, because the fix is in your listing, not your house.


> Thank you for the honest feedback, \[guest first name\]. You're right that the listing didn't make clear \[the stairs to the bedrooms / the road noise from the front rooms / that the pool is shared\]. We've updated the description and added a photo so the next guest knows before they book. We're sorry it came as a surprise.


Then actually update the listing. A response that promises a change the listing doesn't show makes the next guest trust you less.


### Cleanliness


Cleanliness averaged 3.00. Be specific about the process, not just the apology.


> Thank you for telling us, \[guest first name\]. \[Hair in the shower / the dusty ceiling fan / the oven\] isn't the standard we hold, and we've talked it through with our cleaning team. We've added it to the checklist the cleaner signs off with photos after every turnover. We'd be glad to host you again.


"We've added it to the checklist" is stronger than "we're very sorry". It tells the reader the fix runs every time.


### Communication


Communication averaged 3.54 on bad reviews. This one stings, because it's about you rather than the house.


> Thank you, \[guest first name\]. You're right that our reply to your message on \[day\] took too long. That isn't how we want a stay to feel. We've set up \[a second contact for evenings / an AI assistant that answers routine questions any time, with a person on call for urgent ones\], so guests get an answer quickly whatever the hour.


### Check-in


Check-in averaged 3.68, the highest sub-score on bad reviews, but a bad arrival colors everything after it.


> Thank you, \[guest first name\], and we're sorry your arrival was harder than it should have been. \[The keypad code didn't work until we reset it / The directions sent you to the neighbor's driveway\]. We've \[moved to a smart lock that sets a new code for each stay / added a photo of the entrance to the check-in message\], so the next guest gets in on the first try.


If check-in comes up more than once, rewrite the check-in message itself. Our[check-in instructions guide](https://prohost.ai/blog/airbnb-check-in-instructions) has templates for each kind of entry.


### Noise, parties and broken rules


Sometimes the bad review follows you enforcing a rule. The guest was asked to keep it down, or was charged for damage, and the review is the reply. Respond to the facts, never to the person.


> Thank you for staying with us. Our house rules, which every guest agrees to when booking, include quiet hours from \[10 p.m.\] and a maximum of \[number\] guests, because the house is in a residential neighborhood. We contacted the guests on \[date\] when those rules weren't being followed. We're glad to host groups who are looking for a quiet stay.


Don't say "the guest lied" or describe what they did in detail. State the rule, state that you enforced it, and let the reader draw the conclusion. A review written in retaliation for enforcing a rule may also qualify for removal; more on that below.


### "They never told us during the stay"


The hardest review is about a problem you'd have fixed in ten minutes if anyone had told you. Say so, gently.


> Thank you for the feedback, \[guest first name\]. We're sorry the \[Wi-Fi / hot water / heating\] wasn't working as it should. \[We check in with every guest the morning after arrival and\] we're reachable through Airbnb messages any time, and we'd have sent someone right away. We've since \[specific fix\]. For future guests: if anything isn't right, message us and we'll fix it during your stay.


The last line turns "the guest didn't tell us" into "this host fixes things when you tell them".


## What never to write


- **Anything that sounds like a counter-review.** "This guest left the kitchen a mess" belongs in your review of the guest, not in your public response.
- **Private information.** No last names, phone numbers, the guest's reasons for travel, or details from your messages. It's unkind, and it breaks Airbnb's content rules.
- **Refund or compensation details.** "We refunded them $200" invites the next guest to ask for the same.
- **Long explanations.** If your response is longer than the review, it's too long.
- **Promises you haven't kept.** If you say "we've replaced the mattress", replace the mattress first.


## When to dispute instead


A response is for a review that's honest but unflattering. A dispute is for a review that breaks Airbnb's[Reviews Policy](https://www.airbnb.com/help/article/2673) : retaliation, irrelevance, coercion, competitor abuse, or content violations. Airbnb's policy says it generally doesn't mediate disputes about accuracy, and that users can post responses to reviews as long as those responses follow the policy (checked 19 November 2026).


If you think a review qualifies, read[how to remove an Airbnb review](https://prohost.ai/blog/how-to-remove-airbnb-review) first. It covers the five grounds and how to build the case from your guest messages. Our free[Review Dispute Builder](https://prohost.ai/tools/review-dispute-builder) checks a review against those grounds and drafts the message for Airbnb's form. If the review doesn't qualify, come back here and write the response.


You can do both. Keep the response factual, because you don't know how long the review will stay up.


## The private follow-up


Some bad reviews deserve a private message too, especially when the guest had a real problem and you've fixed it. Keep it short and don't ask them to change anything:


> Hi \[guest first name\], thank you again for your review. You were right about \[the issue\], and we've \[fixed it\]. I wanted you to know it made a difference. If you're ever back in \[city\], we'd be glad to host you.


Never offer anything in exchange for changing or removing a review. Airbnb's policy bars it, and it turns a fixable situation into a policy problem.

One response is easy. Every review, every week, on every listing, is where hosts fall behind, and it's why bad reviews get a response about as often as good ones: about 1 in 8.

## FAQ


**Should I respond to every bad review?** Yes, if the review is honest. If the review breaks Airbnb's policy, dispute it, and respond as well.


**How long should a response to a bad review be?** Under 100 words. Four short parts: thanks, the issue, the fix, and a line for the next guest. If your response is longer than the review, cut it.


**How soon should I respond?** Within a few days, once you've decided what to change. A response written in the first hour after reading a bad review is usually the one you'd regret. Leaving it for weeks means more guests read the review with no answer under it.


**Can I edit my response after posting?** Plan as if you can't. Airbnb posts your response immediately. Draft it somewhere else, read it the next morning, then post it.


**Can I ask the guest to change their review?** You can tell them privately what you fixed. Don't ask them to change or remove the review, and never offer anything in return. Airbnb's policy treats that as pressure.


## The takeaway


The guest who left the bad review is gone. The next guest is reading it right now. Write for them: thank the guest, name the issue, say what changed, and give the reader one useful line. Under 100 words, no arguing, no private details. Fix the thing first so the response is true, then make sure every review gets an answer, not just the easy ones.
